academic_source: P007 (Szakmary, Shen & Sharma 2010, JBF) -- mechanism only; exact original parameter grid could not be verified (sciencedirect/researchgate/semanticscholar/repec all blocked by network egress), so standard window pairs (5/20, 10/30, 20/50) were used instead, clearly NOT attributed as the paper's own values

number_of_variants_tested: 18 (3 instruments x 2 timeframes x 3 parameter pairs)
result: NOT ROBUST -- net P&L (base cost scenario) flips sign across the 3 neighbouring parameter pairs in 4 of 6 instrument/timeframe combos (MES 30min: +957/+1623/-3180; MGC 30min: +797/+1005/-3467; MCL 15min: -692/+615/+1867; also directionally mixed). rationale: Non-price-momentum, non-mainstream mechanism per explicit user request: futures term-structure (contango/backwardation) as a return predictor, using real front-vs-next-contract daily prices rather than any price-history indicator (RSI/MACD/MA-crossover family)
academic_source: P009 (Fama & French 1987, J. Business) and P010 (Erb & Harvey 2006, FAJ) -- commodity futures basis/roll-yield risk premium; mechanism only, single-instrument time-series adaptation since this project's 3-instrument universe cannot support the papers' actual cross-sectional design
parameter_family: none (zero free parameters -- sign of basis only, per section 19's preference for simple rules)
result: Net positive in all 3 cost scenarios (base +$4108.16, conservative +$4099.16, stress +$4084.16) and strikingly cost-robust (long holding periods mean transaction costs are a tiny fraction of P&L). BUT only 6 trades over 197 signal-days, because the curve stayed in backwardation 186/197 days (94%) -- nowhere near enough regime changes to say anything statistically. Critically: net P&L is 98.6% of a naive buy-and-hold benchmark over the identical window ($4166.36) -- the strategy cannot be distinguished from simply having been long a market that happened to rally +71% while mostly backwardated. See reports/backtests/ROLL_YIELD_CARRY_v1_MCL.json for the full benchmark comparison.
reason_rejected: Not a demonstrated edge: (1) n=6 trades is even further below section 24's 100+ minimum than prior smoke tests, (2) the result is observationally equivalent to market beta in this sample -- section 21's own reject criteria include results driven by 'one or two huge trades' and this is close kin to that failure mode, (3) the papers' own designs are monthly and/or cross-sectional across a broad commodity panel; a single-instrument daily time-series adaptation is a genuinely different (and untested-in-the-literature) test, not a replication. A real test needs either multi-year data (many independent regime changes) or a broader instrument universe to rank cross-sectionally -- neither available here.
whether_oos_was_viewed: no formal IS/OOS split - sample too small (6 trades) to split meaningfully
whether_idea_was_modified_after_oos: no - zero-parameter specification was fixed before any result was viewed

rationale: Direct user request: session-timed opening-range breakout (London/New York open style), with momentum and/or mean-reversion used only as a FILTER (not the primary signal), volume-confirmed support/resistance, and an internal fear/greed (volatility regime) measure -- tested on both price action AND filter layers together rather than a bare indicator crossover
academic_source: P011 (Zarattini & Aziz 2023, SSRN 4416622) -- mechanism only, citation caveat since all re-verification hosts (SSRN included) were network-blocked; momentum/volume/vol-regime filters are this project's own additions, not from the cited paper
instrument: MES, MGC, MCL (all 3, RTH session only -- no London-session data on disk)
feature_set: opening-bar range [low,high]; first later-bar CLOSE breakout triggers entry at next bar's open, exit at session's own last-bar close; optional filters: momentum (gap alignment), volume (breakout-bar volume > session avg-so-far), vol_regime (FEAR/GREED from trailing-10-session opening-range-width median, an internal realized-vol proxy -- no external VIX data)
parameter_family: vol_regime_lookback=10 sessions (only parameter with a free value; momentum and volume filters are parameter-free directional/threshold rules)
number_of_variants_tested: 36 (3 instruments x 2 bar sizes x 6 filter combinations: none, momentum, volume, momentum+volume, vol_regime=FEAR, vol_regime=GREED)
result: No filter combination shows a robust edge once the 36-cell multiple-comparisons exposure is accounted for. Results are inconsistent in sign across instruments and bar sizes for the same filter (e.g. momentum filter: +$1327 MES 15min, -$600 MGC 15min, +$361 MCL 15min). The single most extreme cell (MGC 30min, vol_regime=GREED: net +$2901, win rate 71%, naive t=2.67 on 28 trades) is the best among all 36 tested cells, but under an uncorrected null, at least one |t|>2.67 among 36 independent draws has roughly a 40% chance even with zero true edge -- consistent with noise, not a finding. Full sweep: reports/backtests/ORB_v1_MES_MGC_MCL_filters.json.
reason_rejected: (1) No filter (momentum, volume, or vol_regime) shows a consistent sign/magnitude across instruments or bar sizes -- the core requirement for treating a filter as a real regime signal rather than a sample-splitting artifact. (2) 36 combinations were swept without any multiple-comparisons correction or held-out validation split, so the single best-looking cell (MGC 30min GREED) cannot be distinguished from a false positive -- same class of error flagged in section 21's reject criteria. (3) Per-cell trade counts (7-67) are far below section 24's 100+ minimum in every case, most severely in the filtered/regime-restricted cells (as few as 7-10 trades). (4) Only RTH (New York) session data was available -- the London-open component of the user's request was not tested at all, a known gap rather than a negative result.
whether_oos_was_viewed: no -- full available sample was used in a single in-sample sweep across all 36 cells; no train/test or walk-forward split was performed
whether_idea_was_modified_after_oos: no formal OOS step existed to modify after; all 36 filter combinations were specified before any result was viewed and none were added or dropped afterward

rationale: Direct fix-attempt for H002's rejection reason (single fast/slow MA pair was fragile, sign-flipped with window choice). Blend multiple independent lookback horizons into a majority-vote consensus signal -- the standard robustness fix for that failure mode, and the one genuinely new mechanism (vs. asset-universe assumptions we can't meet) surfaced from an external strategy-research survey the user brought in this session.
academic_source: P012 (Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen 2012, JFE, time-series momentum) -- mechanism only; the paper's own single 12-month lookback could not be tested (our daily data depth is 199-448 bars per instrument, far short of what a 12-month/252-day lookback needs), so 20/60/120-trading-day lookbacks were used instead; the majority-vote combination across horizons is this project's own construction, not a replication of a specific published voting rule
instrument: MES, MGC, MCL (front contract, daily bars)
feature_set: vote = sum(sign(return_20d), sign(return_60d), sign(return_120d)); LONG if vote>0, SHORT if vote<0, tie skipped; stop-and-reverse, next-bar-open execution
parameter_family: 3 fixed lookback windows (20/60/120 trading days), chosen ex-ante to fit available data depth, not searched/optimized
number_of_variants_tested: 1 specification x 3 instruments x 3 cost scenarios (9 runs), plus a buy-and-hold benchmark per instrument
result: Net POSITIVE in raw dollar terms for all 3 instruments in the base scenario (MES +$3406 on 3 trades, MGC +$7343 on 20 trades, MCL +$646 on 3 trades). But every instrument badly underperforms a same-window buy-and-hold benchmark: MES captured only 84% of buy-and-hold, MGC 49%, MCL 16%. All three instruments happened to trend strongly upward over their available sample windows. Full detail: reports/backtests/MULTI_HORIZON_TREND_v1_MES_MGC_MCL.json.
reason_rejected: Same failure mode as H003 (roll-yield): a nominally positive P&L that is mostly explained by the sample period's own directional drift (a persistent bull run in all 3 instruments over these specific windows), not a demonstrated timing edge -- the strategy's occasional flat/short periods cost more than they saved versus simply staying long. Trade counts (3, 20, 3) are far too small for naive_t_stat (all under 1.0, not HAC-adjusted) to mean anything, consistent with every prior hypothesis in this ledger. The consensus-voting mechanism DOES appear to fix H002's specific complaint (whipsaw/fragility -- it trades far less often and more decisively), but reducing trade frequency in a persistently trending sample necessarily reduces trend capture too, so the fix traded one failure mode for another rather than producing a robust edge.
whether_oos_was_viewed: no formal IS/OOS split -- sample too small (3-20 trades per instrument) to split meaningfully, same limitation as H003
whether_idea_was_modified_after_oos: no -- lookback windows (20/60/120) were fixed ex-ante based on available data depth, before any result was viewed, and not adjusted afterward

rationale: Item #2 from the user-requested strategy-ranking follow-up: apply inverse-realized-vol position sizing on top of H005's multi-horizon trend consensus signal. MES/MGC/MCL are micro contracts specifically sized so graduated position sizing is realistically implementable, not just theoretical.
academic_source: P013 (Barroso & Santa-Clara 2015, JFE, volatility-managed momentum) -- mechanism only (inverse-vol position scaling), not a replication of the paper's own cross-sectional equity-momentum setting, which this project cannot test with 3 futures; citation caveat, network egress blocked all re-verification hosts
instrument: MES, MGC, MCL (front contract, daily bars)
feature_set: same vote signal as H005 (20/60/120-day lookback consensus), position weight = clip(target_daily_vol / trailing-20-day realized vol, 0, 3.0) * sign(vote); continuously rebalanced daily mark-to-market (not discrete stop-and-reverse trades, unlike every other engine in this project)
parameter_family: target_annual_vol=15% (fixed, not fit), vol_lookback=20 days (fixed), max_weight=3.0 cap -- all chosen ex-ante, not optimized
number_of_variants_tested: 1 specification x 3 instruments x 3 cost scenarios (9 runs), plus buy-and-hold benchmark per instrument
result: Net POSITIVE in raw dollar terms for all 3 instruments in base scenario (MES +$1958, MGC +$4619, MCL +$703), but underperforms buy-and-hold even more than the UNSCALED H005 version in 2 of 3 instruments: MES captured only 48% of buy-and-hold (vs H005's 84%), MGC 31% (vs H005's 49%), MCL 17% (vs H005's 16%, roughly unchanged). Full detail: reports/backtests/VOL_SCALED_TREND_v1_and_PORTFOLIO.json.
reason_rejected: Vol-scaling made relative performance WORSE, not better, for 2 of 3 instruments. Mechanism-level explanation: in this sample, the strongest parts of each instrument's rally coincided with elevated realized volatility, so scaling exposure DOWN during high-vol periods capped upside capture during exactly the periods that mattered most for a buy-and-hold comparison -- the same caveat this project's own P013 citation entry flags from later literature. Sharpe-like ratios (0.65 MES, 0.45 MGC, 1.71 MCL) are not meaningfully interpretable given the small, non-independent daily-return samples (78-327 days depending on instrument) and this project's standing skepticism about naive risk-adjusted ratios on small samples.
whether_oos_was_viewed: no formal IS/OOS split -- same limitation as H005, sample too small to split meaningfully
whether_idea_was_modified_after_oos: no -- target_annual_vol/vol_lookback/max_weight were fixed ex-ante before any result was viewed

rationale: Item #3 from the user-requested strategy-ranking follow-up: test whether combining MES (equity index), MGC (gold), and MCL (crude oil) -- three genuinely uncorrelated economic drivers -- into one portfolio produces real diversification benefit, rather than testing one instrument at a time as every prior hypothesis in this ledger has done.
academic_source: General portfolio-diversification principle (Markowitz-style risk reduction from imperfectly correlated return streams); no single paper cited for this specific 3-asset combination, which is this project's own construction given its exact 3-instrument universe
instrument: MES + MGC + MCL combined (front contracts, daily bars)
feature_set: sum of each instrument's H006 (VOL_SCALED_TREND_v1) daily net P&L, aligned by calendar date over the 78-day window where all 3 instruments have a valid signal simultaneously (2026-05-20 to 2026-09-10 -- bounded by MCL's shorter data depth)
parameter_family: none beyond H006's own (no new free parameters -- simple equal-dollar-weight summation across the 3 instruments' existing daily P&L series)
number_of_variants_tested: 1 (single portfolio construction, no weighting scheme search)
result: Real, measurable diversification benefit in RISK terms: daily P&L pairwise correlations were negative or near-zero across all 3 pairs (MES-MGC -0.43, MES-MCL -0.23, MGC-MCL -0.04), and portfolio daily P&L stdev was ~2.1x SMALLER than the naive sum of the 3 instruments' individual stdevs, with portfolio max drawdown ($6,211) much better than the sum of individual max drawdowns ($9,888). But the portfolio's RETURN was net NEGATIVE over this window (-$2,140), while a naive buy-and-hold of the same 3 instruments over the identical window was net POSITIVE (+$176) -- diversification reduced risk exactly as theory predicts, but did not create a return edge where the underlying signal (H006) didn't already have one over this specific window.
reason_rejected: The diversification MECHANISM is validated (real, substantial risk reduction from combining genuinely uncorrelated asset classes) but this is not sufficient on its own to call the strategy a finding: risk-reducing a signal with no demonstrated directional edge does not manufacture an edge, and over the one overlapping window available (only 78 days -- itself a real sample-size limitation driven by MCL's shallower data depth), the combined portfolio lost money while simply holding the same 3 instruments would have made a small profit. A meaningful test of whether this diversification benefit translates into better risk-adjusted RETURNS (not just lower risk) needs a longer overlapping sample than this project's current data depth provides.
whether_oos_was_viewed: no formal IS/OOS split -- 78 overlapping days is too short to split meaningfully
whether_idea_was_modified_after_oos: no -- the portfolio construction (equal-dollar-weight sum, no optimization) was fixed before any result was viewed

rationale: User-requested strategy #2 from a follow-up ranking exercise: a market-neutral front/next spread trade, directly fixing H003 (ROLL_YIELD_CARRY_v1)'s specific failure mode -- H003 traded the front contract outright and was 98.6% explained by buy-and-hold beta. This position (long front/short next or the reverse, equal size) cancels first-order outright exposure by construction, so any result is a real finding about the spread itself, not disguised beta.
academic_source: P015 (Gatev, Goetzmann & Rouwenhorst 2006, RFS, pairs trading) -- mechanism only (hedged spread z-score entry/exit), not a replication of the paper's own cross-sectional equity-pairs setting, which this project cannot test with only 3 futures; citation caveat, network egress blocked all re-verification hosts
feature_set: spread(t) = front_close(t) - next_close(t); z-score vs trailing 20-day mean/stdev; |z|>1.5 opens a hedged spread position (direction per sign of z), |z|<0.25 flattens, otherwise holds
parameter_family: lookback=20, entry_z=1.5, exit_z=0.25 -- fixed ex-ante (standard mean-reversion/pairs-trading convention), not fit to this data
result: Net NEGATIVE in all 3 cost scenarios (base -$313, conservative -$343, stress -$393), only 10 trades (7 short-spread, 3 long-spread) over 199 days, win rate 30%, naive t-stat -0.95. See reports/backtests/SPREAD_MEAN_REV_v1_MCL.json. UPDATE (same session, extended history): re-run on the full 712-bar (~2.9yr) MCL front/next history instead of the original 199-bar slice -- n_trades grew from 10 to 42 (19 long-spread, 23 short-spread), net still NEGATIVE in all 3 scenarios (base -$386, conservative -$512, stress -$722), naive t-stat -1.16 (base). Unlike H009's intraday leg, this extension is NOT compromised by the stale-daily-bar issue found below, since the z-score signal only uses bar-to-bar CLOSE levels, which are genuine even on flat-open bars. See reports/backtests/MCL_EXTENDED_HISTORY_H008_H009.json.
reason_rejected: No edge, and unlike H003 this is a CLEAN negative -- the position is genuinely hedged (long front/short next, equal size), so the loss cannot be blamed on unhedged market beta the way H003's was. The real limiting factor is n=10 trades over the ~9-month window on disk: MCL's own front/next spread simply didn't deviate far enough from its own trailing mean, often enough, to generate a meaningful sample at these fixed thresholds. This is a data-availability limitation (a longer history, or looser entry thresholds, might change this) rather than confirmed absence of the effect -- but as tested, it does not clear this project's bar. UPDATE: the larger, legitimate 42-trade sample confirms the original conclusion rather than overturning it -- still net negative, still no edge, now with 4x the trades so the negative result carries more weight.
whether_oos_was_viewed: no formal IS/OOS split -- n=10 trades is far too small to split meaningfully
whether_idea_was_modified_after_oos: no -- lookback/entry_z/exit_z were fixed before any result was viewed

rationale: User-requested strategy #1 from the same follow-up ranking exercise: decompose each day into overnight (close-to-open) and intraday (open-to-close) legs and test which one, if either, structurally carries the return. Not a trend/momentum/carry variant like H001-H007 -- a question about WHERE return accrues within the day, never tested this session.
academic_source: P014 (Lou, Polk & Skouras 2019, JFE, overnight vs intraday returns) -- mechanism (session-return decomposition) only, original finding is on US equities not futures on gold/oil; citation caveat, network egress blocked all re-verification hosts
instrument: MES, MGC, MCL (front contract, daily bars)
feature_set: overnight leg: BUY at day i-1 close, SELL at day i open, every day; intraday leg: BUY at day i open, SELL at day i close, every day; both always long (descriptive decomposition, not a directional search)
parameter_family: none (zero free parameters -- pure decomposition of already-known open/close prices)
number_of_variants_tested: 2 legs x 3 instruments x 3 cost scenarios (18 runs), plus a chronological split-sample robustness check on the two strongest cells
result: Heterogeneous by instrument. MCL: intraday leg strongly positive (net +$3260 base, t=2.43, captures 78% of buy-and-hold) and CONSISTENT across both halves of the sample when split chronologically (first half t=1.91, second half t=1.66, similar magnitude both times) -- survives the stress cost scenario losing only ~24%. MGC: overnight leg positive (net +$20,156 base, t=1.59, actually EXCEEDS full-period buy-and-hold at 134%) but the split-sample check shows the effect concentrated in the first half (t=2.72 first half vs t=0.52 second half) -- directionally consistent but decaying, not confirmed stable. MES: both legs weak (overnight captures only 42% of buy-and-hold, intraday only 3%), no real finding either direction. Full detail: reports/backtests/SESSION_DECOMP_v1_MES_MGC_MCL.json. UPDATE (same session): attempted to extend the MCL intraday-leg test using the full 712-bar (~2.9yr) MCL history per user request. Discovered a DATA-QUALITY finding instead of a corroborating result: 530/712 (74%) of MCL's daily bars this far back have open==close EXACTLY -- stale single-quote marks, not genuine intraday OHLC (same failure mode already flagged for 4-hour bars in depth_assessment.json, not previously checked at daily resolution this far back). Staleness is heavily front-loaded: quartile 1 is 100% flat, quartile 2 99%, quartile 3 90%, quartile 4 (nearly identical to the original 199-day window) only 9% flat. The intraday leg's open-to-close measurement is structurally zero on a flat bar, so quarters 1-3 cannot provide a fair test -- this is NOT evidence the effect is unstable, it is evidence this data source cannot genuinely extend this SPECIFIC test further back than ~9 months. See data/metadata/depth_assessment.json (second_revision_daily_bar_staleness) and reports/backtests/MCL_EXTENDED_HISTORY_H008_H009.json. HAC RECHECK (same session, after H015): added a Newey-West HAC-adjusted significance module (futures_quant/research/significance.py) -- every prior t-stat in this ledger was naive (i.i.d.-assuming). Applied to MCL's intraday leg (n=199, the strongest still-standing result): naive t=2.43 shrinks to HAC t=2.19 (lag=1), 2.06 (Newey-West rule-of-thumb lag=4), 2.03 (lag=5), 2.01 (lag=10) -- modest shrinkage from autocorrelation correction, but the result STAYS ABOVE the conventional 1.96 two-tailed significance threshold at every lag tested, 1 through 10. This is the first result in this project's ledger to survive a genuine autocorrelation-robust significance check, not just a naive one -- it does not become a confirmed finding (still short/absolute sample by academic standards, no true held-out OOS period, HAC corrects autocorrelation but not the underlying short-sample-window limitation), but it is now the single most rigorously-vetted result in this ledger. MGC's overnight leg (n=447, previously flagged as decaying/not confirmed via the split-sample check) was also re-checked for consistency: naive t=1.59, HAC t=1.63/1.62/1.57 across lags 1/5/10 -- barely moves and stays below 1.96 either way, no change to its rejected status. See reports/backtests/HAC_SIGNIFICANCE_RECHECK.json.
reason_rejected: MCL's intraday-leg result is NOT rejected -- it is the first result in this project's hypothesis ledger that (a) beats a meaningful fraction of buy-and-hold, (b) has a trade count (199, ~100 per half) above the levels every other rejected hypothesis was flagged for being short of, (c) has the highest naive t-stat of anything tested this session (2.43), and (d) is CONSISTENT in both magnitude and significance across a chronological split-sample check, the strongest robustness signal available given current data depth. It is marked provisional rather than a demonstrated edge because naive_t_stat is still not HAC/Newey-West adjusted, the sample (199 days) is still short by absolute academic standards, and no true out-of-sample period exists beyond the split check. MGC's overnight-leg result and MES's results (both legs) ARE rejected on this project's standing criteria: MGC's apparent edge fails the split-sample stability check (front-loaded, decaying), and MES shows no meaningful effect either direction. UPDATE: the MCL intraday leg's original t=2.43 result on the 199-day window is UNCHANGED (same data, not re-run) and remains the strongest result in this ledger, but its 'provisional pass' status cannot be upgraded to a confirmed finding via more IBKR history, because no further genuine history exists for this specific test through this connector. Status stays provisional, now with an explicit note that this connector has hit its real ceiling for corroborating this particular hypothesis -- a longer, independent out-of-sample period would need an external data vendor (Databento, CME DataMine, Barchart per section 14), not more calls to this connector.
whether_oos_was_viewed: a chronological split-sample check was performed (not a true held-out OOS period, since both halves come from the same already-analyzed dataset) -- MCL intraday held up across the split; MGC overnight did not
whether_idea_was_modified_after_oos: no -- the split-sample check was performed on the specification exactly as it produced the full-sample result, with no parameter changes; it decreased confidence in MGC's result and increased confidence in MCL's, but did not alter the underlying rule being tested

rationale: User-cited retail trading heuristic: 'buy [instrument] at market open, sell the next day, repeat daily.' Originally cited for Micron (MU), a stock this project has no data or infrastructure for -- tested here as the analogous mechanism on MES/MGC/MCL, the only instruments this project covers. New third leg ('extended') added to the SESSION_DECOMP_v1 engine: buy today's open, sell tomorrow's open, as ONE continuous position (single round-trip cost per day) rather than H009's two separate overnight+intraday legs.
academic_source: No specific academic paper -- this is a user-supplied retail trading heuristic, not a published strategy. Tested on its own terms as a mechanically well-defined rule.
instrument: MES, MGC, MCL (front contract, daily bars; MCL uses the extended ~2.9yr history since this leg is NOT affected by the open==close staleness issue found testing H009 -- opens genuinely differ day-to-day even in the 'stale' quarters, confirmed by direct check)
feature_set: buy at day i's open, sell at day i+1's open, every day, always long (zero parameters, zero signal -- this IS the entire heuristic as stated)
number_of_variants_tested: 1 specification x 3 instruments x 3 cost scenarios (9 runs), plus a buy-and-hold benchmark per instrument
result: Net POSITIVE in the base scenario for MES (+$2857, 71% of buy-and-hold) and MGC (+$13,771, 92% of buy-and-hold), roughly breakeven for MCL (+$293, only 10% of buy-and-hold). Under the conservative/stress scenarios MCL turns net NEGATIVE (-$774, -$2551) and both MES and MGC degrade substantially. naive_t_stat never exceeds 0.94 (MGC base) across any instrument/scenario -- the strongest cell is still weaker than the weakest 'promising' result elsewhere in this ledger. See reports/backtests/H010_H011_MES_MGC_MCL.json.
reason_rejected: This heuristic is MATHEMATICALLY INCAPABLE of beating a true buy-and-hold on the same instrument, and the backtest confirms this structurally rather than just empirically: buying at open and selling at the next open, repeated daily, captures essentially the SAME cumulative price change as holding continuously from the first day's open to the last day's close (both are just 'the total move over the period'), but the daily version pays a full round-trip transaction cost EVERY SINGLE DAY while buy-and-hold pays it ONCE. Every instrument's ratio_to_benchmark is below 1.0 for exactly this reason -- the heuristic isn't a bad directional bet, it's an identical directional bet to buy-and-hold with unnecessary daily costs added on top. As stated (unconditional, no signal, no exit rule), this heuristic can only equal buy-and-hold in a zero-cost world and must underperform it in any real one. It would only become genuinely different from buy-and-hold if paired with an actual entry/exit SIGNAL (skip some days, reverse on others) -- which is a different, untested hypothesis, not this one.
whether_oos_was_viewed: no formal IS/OOS split -- not needed here since the result follows from cost arithmetic, not a fitted pattern that could overfit
whether_idea_was_modified_after_oos: no -- the rule (buy open, sell next open, every day) was tested exactly as stated by the user, unconditionally, before any result was viewed

rationale: First genuinely intermarket test this session: does one instrument's daily return predict the NEXT day's return in a DIFFERENT instrument? All prior hypotheses (H001-H010) are single-instrument mechanisms. This project's 3 instruments span 3 different asset classes (equity index, gold, crude oil) with plausible economic linkages (oil feeding inflation expectations relevant to both equities and gold; gold as a risk-off/flight-to-quality signal for equity sentiment) worth testing directly rather than assuming.
academic_source: No single paper cited -- this project's own construction testing a general intermarket-propagation-with-lag principle (well established qualitatively in intermarket analysis and commodity-as-leading-indicator literature) on this project's specific 3-instrument universe, not a replication of any specific published test.
instrument: All 6 directed pairs among MES, MGC, MCL (leader -> target)
feature_set: sign(leader's close-to-close return on day t) -> trade target LONG/SHORT at target's day t+1 open, exit at day t+1 close (intraday hold); zero-return leader days skipped
parameter_family: none (zero free parameters beyond which pair is tested)
number_of_variants_tested: 6 directed pairs x base cost scenario (6 runs)
result: No pair shows a robust positive result. MES->MGC: +$3825, t=0.55. MCL->MES: +$2467, t=1.03 (the best of the 6, still weak). The other 4 pairs are net NEGATIVE: MES->MCL -$2573 (t=-1.88), MGC->MES -$3501 (t=-1.45), MGC->MCL -$2618 (t=-1.90), MCL->MGC -$7948 (t=-1.14). Notably, BOTH pairs targeting MCL from MES or MGC are meaningfully negative (t=-1.88, -1.90) with similar magnitude -- suggestive of a possible INVERSE relationship (MES/MGC up -> MCL down next day) rather than the co-movement this hypothesis actually tested, but that inverse direction was NOT itself tested and is flagged as a candidate for a future hypothesis, not claimed as a finding here. See reports/backtests/H010_H011_MES_MGC_MCL.json.
reason_rejected: None of the 6 same-direction pairs clears any meaningful bar (all |t| < 2, most below 1). Two pairs are directionally interesting in aggregate (both MCL-targeting-negative pairs share sign and similar magnitude) but that specific inverse hypothesis was not tested here and testing it now on the same data, having already seen this pattern, would be exactly the kind of post-hoc data-mining this project's own hypothesis-ledger discipline exists to prevent -- it needs to be proposed and tested as its own fresh hypothesis (ideally with an economic rationale established BEFORE looking at the result, which the current one only found by pattern-matching after the fact).
whether_oos_was_viewed: no formal IS/OOS split -- 6 pairs on one sample each, no split performed
whether_idea_was_modified_after_oos: no -- all 6 directed pairs were specified and run identically before any result was viewed; the inverse-relationship observation was noted AFTER seeing results and is explicitly NOT being claimed as tested

rationale: User request: 'try crypto, be creative.' Added CME Micro Bitcoin futures (MBT) as a 4th data source -- not traded, only used as a cross-asset LEADER signal for MES/MGC/MCL via the existing CROSS_ASSET_LEAD_LAG_v1 engine (H011, reused as-is). Creative angle: real BTC/USD trades 24/7 but CME's MBT futures close for the weekend like every other CME product, so MBT's own Friday-to-Monday gap is the one place in this project's data where a genuinely 24/7 market's non-trading-day information (crypto reacting to weekend news while every other instrument here is shut) becomes visible as a single jump -- tested whether that weekend gap carries MORE cross-asset signal than an ordinary weekday move, by splitting results into Monday-execution vs other-weekday trades.
academic_source: No specific paper cited -- general principle that crypto (as the only continuously-traded, retail-and-macro-sensitive asset in reach) may reflect risk-sentiment shifts faster than markets that are closed; this project's own construction and first-ever crypto test, not a replication.
instrument: Leader: MBT (CME Micro Bitcoin futures, front contract, daily bars, 2025-03-31 to 2026-09-11). Targets: MES, MGC, MCL.
feature_set: sign(MBT close-to-close return on day t) -> LONG/SHORT target at target's day t+1 open, exit at day t+1 close (same mechanism as H011, MBT substituted as leader)
parameter_family: none (zero free parameters beyond which target is tested)
number_of_variants_tested: 3 targets x 3 cost scenarios (9 runs), each split into Monday-execution vs other-weekday subgroups, plus a chronological split-sample robustness check and a data-quality-restricted re-run for the standout result (MBT->MCL)
result: MBT->MGC is the strongest pooled result of any lead-lag pair tested this session (net +$10,656 base, t=1.53, actually stronger across weekdays generally than specifically on Mondays -- t=1.42 other-weekday vs 0.59 Monday, so NOT a weekend-specific effect for gold). MBT->MES is weak (t=0.59) but IS somewhat Monday-concentrated (t=0.83 Monday vs 0.21 other-weekday) on a small subsample (48 Monday trades). MBT->MCL is strongly NEGATIVE (net -$2849 base, t=-2.06, the most extreme t-stat of this entire session in the initial full-window run) -- but a chronological split-sample check revealed this was partly a DATA-QUALITY ARTIFACT: the first half of trades landed almost entirely in MCL's known-stale pre-2025-12-26 window (already flagged in H009 -- MCL bars there are mostly open==close, meaning the intraday-hold execution used here produces a near-guaranteed small cost-only loss on most of those 'trades', explaining an implausible 3.9% win rate in that half). Re-run restricted to MCL's verified-clean window (2025-12-26 onward, 176 trades, only 16/178 bars flat) still shows a negative, moderately significant result (t=-1.70 base, -2.21 stress) -- the negative relationship survives on trustworthy data, just weaker than the inflated pooled headline number. See reports/backtests/H012_CRYPTO_LEAD_LAG_MBT.json. FOLLOW-UP (H013, same session): testing the inverse direction and decomposing both by long/short P&L revealed this result is substantially explained by MCL's own strong directional drift over the clean window (buy-and-hold +$4250) interacting with the original signal's short-heavy bias (94 short / 82 long trades) -- shorts alone lost -$3110, longs alone were +$795. This is very likely BETA EXPOSURE, not a genuine BTC->MCL information relationship. Confidence in this finding should be revised down substantially; see H013 for the full diagnostic.
reason_rejected: None of the three pairs is a demonstrated edge. MBT->MGC has the best pooled t-stat of the session (1.53) but is NOT explained by the creative 'weekend information' mechanism this hypothesis actually proposed (the effect is not Monday-concentrated), so even if real, it would need a different explanation than the one tested. MBT->MES's Monday-concentration is suggestive but rests on only 48 Monday trades, too few to trust. MBT->MCL survived a genuine robustness check (data-staleness-corrected re-run) with a real, if weaker, negative result (t=-1.70 to -2.21 on the clean window) -- this is the most carefully-verified negative finding of the session, and its inverse (long MCL / short MCL as a function of BTC direction, flipped) is flagged as a legitimate candidate for a FUTURE hypothesis, not tested here to avoid post-hoc data-mining on the same sample (same discipline applied to H011's analogous pattern).
whether_oos_was_viewed: a chronological split-sample check was performed on MBT->MCL specifically (triggered by an implausible subgroup win rate, not planned in advance) -- this is exactly the kind of after-the-fact robustness check this project's own discipline calls for, and it correctly caught a real data-quality contamination rather than confirming a clean effect
whether_idea_was_modified_after_oos: yes, in one specific documented way: after finding MBT->MCL's first-half win rate was implausible (3.9%), the target series was restricted to MCL's already-known-clean date range (established independently in H009, not fit to this result) and re-run -- this is a data-quality correction using a PRE-EXISTING, independently-derived cutoff date, not a parameter tuned to improve this hypothesis's own result

rationale: User-requested direct follow-up to H012: test the mirror of the MBT->MCL relationship (LONG MCL when BTC's prior-day return is negative, SHORT when positive), since H012's verified-clean-window result was negative (BTC up -> MCL down). Pre-registered: the direction to test was fixed by H012's own already-established sign, not searched for after seeing this test's own result. Added invert=True to CROSS_ASSET_LEAD_LAG_v1's engine/strategy (generate_lead_lag_signals, run_cross_asset_lead_lag_backtest) to flip the direction mapping cleanly, reusing all existing signal/execution logic.
academic_source: Same as H012 -- no specific paper, this project's own construction testing whether the H012 relationship is exploitable in the mirror direction.
instrument: Leader: MBT (CME Micro Bitcoin futures). Target: MCL, both full window and the verified-clean window (>=2025-12-26, per H009/H012).
feature_set: sign(MBT close-to-close return on day t), INVERTED -> LONG target when leader NEGATIVE, SHORT when leader POSITIVE; executed at target's next-day open-to-close (same mechanism as H012, direction flipped)
number_of_variants_tested: 1 (inverted direction) x 2 windows (full, clean) x 3 cost scenarios (6 runs), plus a long/short P&L decomposition and an MCL buy-and-hold benchmark for both the original and inverted direction on the clean window
result: Clean-window inverted result is only weakly POSITIVE (t=0.76 base, 0.56 conservative, 0.24 stress on 176 trades) -- nowhere near as strong as H012's original clean-window NEGATIVE result (t=-1.70 to -2.21) was. This asymmetry has two causes, both now verified: (1) transaction costs are direction-agnostic (same $ round-trip cost whichever way a trade goes), so an exact direction-flip does NOT simply negate net P&L -- the inverse has to overcome the same cost drag fresh, mechanically producing a weaker mirror result even with a perfectly symmetric true edge; (2) a genuine confound -- the clean window's original (non-inverted) trades were 94 short / 82 long, and MCL rallied hard over this window (buy-and-hold +$4250), so the short-heavy original signal lost heavily on its short trades specifically (-$3110 from 94 shorts) while its few longs did fine (+$795 from 82 longs) -- the SAME pattern of shorts-lose/longs-win appears in the inverted version too (shorts -$1391, longs +$2426), meaning both the original and inverted results are substantially explained by MCL's own directional drift interacting with how often the signal happens to say long vs short, not by genuine information flowing from BTC to MCL. See reports/backtests/H013_INVERSE_BTC_MCL.json.
reason_rejected: The inverse is not a demonstrated edge (t<1 in every scenario). More importantly, this test's own diagnostic work meaningfully DOWNGRADES confidence in H012's original MBT->MCL finding: what looked like a real, split-sample-verified negative relationship is now better explained as beta exposure (shorting into a persistent MCL rally) combined with a signal that happened to be short-biased during this specific window, rather than crude oil genuinely reacting to Bitcoin's direction. This is the same contamination pattern that killed H003/H005/H006/H007 earlier in this ledger, just discovered one hypothesis later than usual because the market-neutral framing of a cross-asset LEAD-LAG test does not make it automatically beta-free the way H008's explicitly hedged spread trade was -- a lesson worth keeping for any future intermarket hypothesis in this project: check the long/short trade balance and compare against buy-and-hold before trusting a lead-lag result, not just its t-stat.
whether_oos_was_viewed: no new out-of-sample data was used -- same clean window as H012, direction flipped and long/short P&L decomposed
whether_idea_was_modified_after_oos: no -- invert=True was the single pre-specified change, decided before this test was run, not tuned in response to this test's own result. The long/short decomposition that revealed the beta confound was diagnostic analysis, not a modification of the hypothesis being tested.

rationale: User proposal: test breakout during the London and NY session opens, with the user's own explicit skepticism that this may not apply to futures since CME/COMEX products trade ~23h/day (no literal overnight order backlog releasing into a gap the way an equity market open works). NY-open breakout was already tested via H004 (ORB_v1, RTH-session first-bar opening range) and rejected as noise. London-open had never been tested -- no outside_rth=true data existed on disk (all prior intraday fetches used outside_rth=false, RTH-only). Rather than build a full London-open breakout strategy on an assumed premise, first did a direct empirical premise check: does MGC (gold, the instrument most plausibly linked to London trading hours via the London gold fix) actually show a volume/volatility cluster around the London open, the way ORB's economic rationale requires?
academic_source: No specific paper -- direct empirical premise check on this project's own fresh IBKR data, testing the general session-liquidity-clustering principle (regional cash-market open hours drive futures volume/volatility even without a literal trading halt) before committing to build a full strategy on it.
timeframe: 15min, outside_rth=true (first-ever non-RTH fetch this project; all prior intraday data was RTH-only)
feature_set: hour-of-day (UTC) average bar volume and average high-low range, computed over the full available outside_rth=true window (1000 bars, 2026-08-28 to 2026-09-14, ~17 calendar days -- the outside_rth=true window is SHORTER than the RTH-only ~46-day/1000-bar depth, since 24h/day bars consume the same 1000-bar cap faster) and independently on a chronological split-half (first vs second ~8.5 days) as a robustness check.
parameter_family: none -- purely descriptive (no strategy parameters), a go/no-go premise check performed BEFORE any strategy code was written
result: PREMISE REJECTED. London open (~07:00-08:00 UTC during BST, when London's cash gold/FX markets open) shows LOW volume/range in MGC -- avg volume 238-321 contracts/bar, among the weakest hours of the day, in BOTH halves of the sample independently (half1: 266/409, half2: 216/248). By contrast, the NY cash equity open window (~12:00-14:00 UTC, 9:00-10:00am ET, overlapping COMEX floor open ~8:20am ET) is unambiguously the dominant volume/volatility cluster of the entire 23h session -- avg volume 890-1102 contracts/bar (2.7x-4.6x the London-open hours), avg range $15.9-$17.6 (roughly double the daily average), and this holds consistently in both the first half (945/1314/1423) and second half (826/848/597) of the sample. The daily maintenance break (21:00 UTC, 5-6pm ET) shows correctly as zero bars, confirming the data is sound. A spot-check for holiday distortion (Sep 7 Labor Day, one of 12 trading days) showed reduced volume that single day but did not change the hourly pattern qualitatively.
reason_rejected: The economic mechanism this hypothesis actually needed (a London-session liquidity/volatility bump distinct from and comparable to the NY-open bump) is not present in gold futures in this data -- NY-open dominance is overwhelming and consistent across both halves of the sample, while London-open shows no elevation at all above the broader Asian/European overnight baseline. Building a London-open ORB variant on this instrument would be testing a strategy whose own economic premise already failed a direct empirical check -- exactly the kind of avoidable dead end this project's discipline is meant to catch before spending backtest effort on it. This does NOT contradict the user's original skepticism about futures trading ~23h/day (which was about the literal gap-breakout mechanism); it goes further and shows even the weaker liquidity-clustering version of the idea does not hold for MGC around London hours specifically, in the one short window this connector could currently serve. Caveat: sample is short (~17 days, 44 bars/hour) and single-instrument (only MGC tested, chosen for its plausible London linkage) -- this is a premise check, not a definitive claim that no futures product ever shows a London-open effect, but it is enough to not proceed to a full H014 strategy build on MGC specifically.
whether_oos_was_viewed: no formal IS/OOS split -- this is a premise check, not a strategy backtest; the chronological split-half was used only to confirm the hour-of-day pattern itself was not an artifact of one sub-period
whether_idea_was_modified_after_oos: no -- the premise check (hour-of-day volume/range) was specified before being run, and NY-open vs London-open were both examined identically; no strategy was built or modified based on this result, it was used exactly as intended, as a gate on whether to proceed

rationale: User follow-up after H014's rejected London-open premise check: 'add volume related stuff' (open-ended). Selected the High-Volume Return Premium (Gervais, Kaniel & Mingelgrin 2001, JF, P016) -- an instrument's own trading VOLUME relative to its trailing average, independent of that day's own price direction, as a standalone directional signal. First hypothesis this session where the signal is trading ACTIVITY rather than price (H001-H014 were all price-based: returns, moving averages, term structure, session decomposition, breakouts). Discovered and fixed a data-quality bug while building this: the previously-persisted MCL 'full history' daily CSV (data/raw/MCL/MCLV6_1day_20231023_20260911_full.csv) had volume=0.0 in EVERY row -- a save-script bug, not an IBKR gap (a live re-fetch confirmed real, ramping, non-zero MCL daily volume exists, e.g. 137837 on 2026-09-04). Corrected with a fresh clean-window fetch (data/raw/MCL/MCLV6_1day_20251224_20260911_clean_with_volume.csv). MES and MGC's already-persisted daily CSVs were independently verified to already have genuine volume.
academic_source: P016 (Gervais, Kaniel & Mingelgrin 2001, Journal of Finance 56(3), 877-919, DOI 10.1111/0022-1082.00349) -- mechanism only (investor-recognition/attention-grabbing hypothesis: unusual volume increases visibility, drawing subsequent demand); original paper is US equities over 1963-1996, exact reported numbers not independently re-verifiable (network egress blocked, same standing caveat as every other paper this session). Adapted here as a simple threshold rule (trailing-20-day volume ratio >= 1.5x -> LONG, <= 1/1.5x -> SHORT), not the original decile-sort methodology.
instrument: MES (MESZ6), MGC (MGCV6), MCL (MCLV6, clean window only)
feature_set: volume_ratio(t) = volume(t) / trailing_20day_avg_volume(t), baseline strictly excludes day t itself; signal fires when ratio >= 1.5 (LONG) or <= 0.667 (SHORT); executed at day t+1's open, held a FIXED number of trading days, exited at that day's close
parameter_family: holding_period in {10, 20} trading days x non_overlapping in {False (all signals, overlapping holds allowed), True (mutually-exclusive trades only)} x 3 cost scenarios, per instrument (12 backtests per instrument, 36 total)
result: STRIKING DIVERGENCE between overlapping and non-overlapping variants -- and this divergence IS the finding. Overlapping (all signals, holding windows allowed to stack): looks spectacular everywhere -- MES 10d: 144 trades, net +$24,600 (6.4x buy&hold), t=2.51; MES 20d: 140 trades, net +$31,059 (8.1x buy&hold), t=2.23; MGC 10d: 165 trades, net +$40,067 (2.6x buy&hold), t=1.37; MCL 10d: 93 trades, net +$11,432 (2.7x buy&hold), t=1.83. Non-overlapping (mutually-exclusive trades only, the methodologically defensible cut): the effect either becomes statistically insignificant, collapses to a tiny untrustworthy sample, or REVERSES SIGN. MES 10d: 19 trades, t=0.58 (not significant), ratio 0.64 (underperforms buy&hold). MES 20d: only 10 trades, t=2.54, ratio 1.86 -- intriguing but n=10 is far below this project's 100-trade floor and contradicts its own 10-day-hold result on the SAME instrument (t=0.58), a classic multiple-comparisons red flag. MGC 10d: 26 trades, net -$2,026, t=-0.17 (sign FLIPS negative). MGC 20d: 13 trades, net -$3,132, t=-0.23 (also flips negative). MCL 10d: 14 trades, net +$1,372, t=0.72 (weak positive, ratio only 0.33 of buy&hold). MCL 20d: 7 trades, net -$477, t=-0.17 (flips negative). A second confound also visible in EVERY overlapping result: LONG trades captured almost all the profit while SHORT trades lost money (e.g. MGC 10d: longs +$54,301 vs shorts -$14,234; MCL 10d: longs +$17,588 vs shorts -$6,155) -- the same long/short asymmetry pattern H013 found explained H012's apparent MBT->MCL edge as beta exposure rather than genuine signal, and all 3 instruments had a net-positive buy-and-hold over these windows, consistent with the overlapping numbers partly just re-counting the same underlying uptrend many times over via redundant overlapping windows rather than reflecting real volume-shock alpha. See reports/backtests/H015_VOLUME_SHOCK_MES_MGC_MCL.json for the full 36-row table. HAC RECHECK (same session): the MES 20d/non-overlapping cell (n=10, already flagged as too thin to trust and inconsistent with its own 10-day-hold sibling result) was re-checked with the new HAC significance module out of consistency, not because it looked promising. Its HAC t-stat actually INCREASES at every testable lag (naive t=2.54 -> HAC t=3.23 at lag=1, 3.52 at lag=2, 3.81 at lag=5; lag=10 is undefined since lag>=n at n=10). This is NOT evidence the effect is real -- with only 10 observations, a HAC covariance estimate has far too few effective degrees of freedom to be a trustworthy correction (Newey-West's asymptotic theory assumes n large relative to the chosen lag), so an erratic, lag-sensitive swing in either direction is exactly what small-n HAC estimation produces, not a signal. This cell stays rejected for the same reason it always was (n=10, below this project's 100-trade floor, inconsistent across holding periods) -- HAC is not a substitute for sample size, and this result is flagged explicitly as an example of that rather than quietly dropped. See reports/backtests/HAC_SIGNIFICANCE_RECHECK.json.
reason_rejected: The overlapping-window 'headline' numbers (t>2, multiples of buy-and-hold) are a METHODOLOGICAL ARTIFACT, not a real edge: with a 10-20 day hold and near-daily signal cadence, up to 19 signal days can have trades open simultaneously, so naive_t_stat's independent-observations assumption is badly violated and the same underlying price moves get counted into many overlapping 'trades' at once, inflating both apparent PnL and apparent significance. The non-overlapping (mutually-exclusive-trades) cut is the methodologically honest test, and on that cut the effect is not significant (MES 10d, MCL 10d/20d), reverses sign entirely (MGC both holding periods), or survives only in one thin, sample-starved, holding-period-inconsistent cell (MES 20d, n=10) that looks exactly like what a stricter multiple-comparisons standard is supposed to catch, not a discovery to chase further. This does not reject the underlying academic literature (tested on a 33-year individual-equity sample by the original authors, not 3 futures contracts over well under 2 years) -- it says this project's own adaptation, on its own data, does not show a trustworthy volume-shock edge, and specifically flags that ANY future hypothesis in this project using a multi-day holding period with daily (or more frequent) signal generation needs a non-overlapping/mutually-exclusive-trades check as a standard robustness step, not an optional extra -- this is the first hypothesis this session structured to actually run that check, and it's the reason the rejection is confident rather than ambiguous.
whether_oos_was_viewed: no formal IS/OOS split -- the non-overlapping vs overlapping comparison served as this hypothesis's primary robustness check (analogous to H009's chronological split and H012's clean-window re-run), not a held-out period
whether_idea_was_modified_after_oos: no -- both non_overlapping modes, both holding periods, and all 3 cost scenarios were run identically and reported in full (36 rows, all in the report file) before any selective interpretation; the MES 20d/non-overlapping cell's weak (n=10) result is flagged as untrustworthy in the same report rather than being pulled out and presented as a finding

rationale: User-specified 'traditional' technical-analysis system: price-structure breakout (higher-high/higher-low) + MACD trend confirmation ("MACD going up ... above ... x%") + a moving-average extension filter, with MACD's own crossover as the exit/reverse trigger ("take profit when it turns down cross down and short"). Operationalized higher-high/higher-low as a Donchian-style N-day breakout (close above/below the prior N-day high/low) rather than literal fractal swing-point detection, to avoid look-ahead/arbitrary-lag issues while capturing the same market-structure idea; used standard MACD(12,26,9) (Gerald Appel's original parameters, not fit to data); added an SMA(50) extension filter requiring price to clear the MA by a threshold percent before entry is allowed.
academic_source: P017 (Brock, Lakonishok & LeBaron 1992, JF, moving-average/breakout rules -- mechanism) and P018 (Sullivan, Timmermann & White 2001, JF, data-snooping bootstrap correction on the SAME finding -- methodological caution). MACD itself is Gerald Appel's practitioner indicator (late 1970s), not from a peer-reviewed paper; its standard (12,26,9) parameters used as the universal default.
feature_set: close[t] > prior-20-day high (LONG breakout) or < prior-20-day low (SHORT breakout), AND MACD line > signal line AND MACD line > 0 (LONG) [mirror for SHORT], AND close >= SMA(50)*(1+extension_pct) [mirror for SHORT]; entry only when ALL THREE agree simultaneously. Exit/reverse ONLY on a MACD line/signal crossover in the opposite direction -- not when the breakout or extension condition merely stops holding.
parameter_family: extension_pct in {1%, 2% (user's own suggestion), 3%} -- a small, pre-registered 3-value grid bracketing the user's suggestion, NOT a wide search, per P018's standing data-snooping caution. breakout_lookback=20, ma_window=50, MACD=(12,26,9) held fixed at standard textbook values throughout, never varied.
result: Requiring breakout + MACD + MA-extension to ALL agree simultaneously is a very selective filter -- trade counts are tiny everywhere: MES 3-8 trades (depending on extension_pct), MGC 14-16, MCL exactly 7 at every threshold tested. naive_t_stat NEVER exceeds 0.99 across all 27 runs (MES: 0.06-0.65; MGC: 0.63-0.99; MCL: -0.02 to -0.17, i.e. slightly NEGATIVE at every threshold). Net P&L is positive for MES ($219-$1289) and MGC ($4691-$6997) but substantially UNDERPERFORMS simple buy-and-hold on the same instrument (best ratio_to_benchmark: MES 0.34, MGC 0.46 -- sitting mostly flat/out-of-market when the 3-way filter isn't satisfied forfeits most of the instrument's own drift). MCL is net NEGATIVE at every extension_pct tested (-$25 to -$260). See reports/backtests/H016_MACD_SWING_BREAKOUT_MES_MGC_MCL.json for the full 27-row table.
reason_rejected: Every cell fails on at least one, usually all, of this project's standing bars: (1) trade counts (3-16) are far below the 100-trade floor used throughout this ledger to flag a result as too thin to trust -- MES's 3-trade cell in particular is not a statistical test of anything; (2) no naive_t_stat comes remotely close to conventional significance (max 0.99, nowhere near ~2), so a HAC re-check (per the project's new significance module) was not even run -- it would only shrink an already-non-significant number further, and on n=7-16 a HAC estimate would itself be unreliable, the same small-n caution already flagged for H015's thin cell; (3) where positive, the strategy underperforms doing nothing more sophisticated than buying and holding the same instrument, meaning the elaborate 3-condition filter is net COUNTERPRODUCTIVE relative to the baseline it should be trying to beat; (4) MCL is negative outright. This is exactly the pattern P018 warns about: a plausible-sounding, textbook-standard technical combination, tested honestly on real data with a small pre-registered parameter set (not a search), simply does not clear the bar. Rejected.
whether_oos_was_viewed: no formal IS/OOS split -- naive_t_stat was clearly non-significant everywhere (max 0.99), so a split-sample or HAC check (both used elsewhere in this ledger to corroborate a PROMISING result) was not warranted here; there was nothing promising to corroborate
whether_idea_was_modified_after_oos: no -- breakout_lookback=20, ma_window=50, and MACD=(12,26,9) were fixed before any result was viewed; extension_pct's 3-value grid (1%/2%/3%) was chosen to bracket the user's own suggested 2% before running, not selected afterward, and all 27 cells are reported in full rather than only the least-bad one
